r: GIS 1220 introduces the conceptual foundations of geospatial technology: maps, GPS, geographic information science, and remote sensing, plus basic spatial problem-solving and interpretation of visualizations. These are Computer and Mathematical-adjacent tasks, and observed-usage data shows that category dominates current AI use, meaning AI already competently answers conceptual GIS questions and interprets basic spatial data. Yet the course carries a Natural and Physical Sciences General Studies designation, a GT-Pathways-level transfer mandate, and its own description states that intermediate spatial analysis skills are taken up in subsequent GIS courses, marking it explicit scaffolding for the geospatial sequence including GIS 2710 and GIS 2250. At 24 months, the instrumental need to build this conceptual substrate is not eroded: AI can define GPS accuracy or explain remote sensing, but students still need the underlying vocabulary to use GIS tools and advance in the major. Foundational role and transfer designation hold the rating at Low.

By 2031, AI tutoring systems will likely explain geospatial concepts, GPS principles, and remote sensing fluently, and could walk a student through basic spatial problem-solving interactively; Computer and Mathematical tasks remain the largest observed-usage category and continue growing. The instrumental case for lecture-based delivery of these concepts erodes, since AI can already answer how GPS trilateration works competently. But the course's foundational-scaffolding role, feeding GIS 2710, GIS 2250, and the rest of the geospatial curriculum, and its Natural Sciences General Studies mandate persist as caps on the rating rather than disappearing with capability gains. The instrumental need for a novice to master vocabulary and mental models before touching intermediate GIS software is largely unaffected by better AI question-answering. The rating rises to Medium: content delivery is increasingly automatable, but the substrate role for the sequence and the general-education requirement keep it from reaching High.

A decade out, capability trends suggest AI will handle nearly all conceptual explanation and basic problem-solving this course covers, given the roughly four-to-seven-month doubling in AI task-time-horizons implies dramatically more capable tutoring and question-answering systems by 2036. The execution rationale for a human-taught introductory course is substantially eroded on the pure content-delivery dimension. Still, the course's foundational-scaffolding role for the whole geospatial-technology sequence and its likely persistence as a Natural and Physical Sciences transfer requirement continue to cap the rating at Medium rather than High; a foundational course is not eliminated merely because its content becomes easier to deliver. The genuine uncertainty is pedagogical: how introductory GIS is taught when AI can answer every conceptual question, not whether the entry-level scaffolding function itself disappears. This is a directional judgment, not a confident point-prediction, given how far out the horizon sits.
GIS 1220.d: This course serves as an introduction to technologies used for visualization, measurement, and analysis of geographical features that occur on earth. Students learn basic concepts needed to understand maps, global positioning system (GPS), geographic information science (GIS) and remote sensing of the environment. Topics include the nature and characteristics of geospatial technologies, concepts of spatial data, principles and methods of capturing and representing spatial data, and methods of analysis and interpretation of maps and visualizations. This course addresses basic analysis and spatial problem-solving skills. Intermediate spatial analysis skills are taken up in subsequent GIS courses.

r: GIS 2250 is explicitly described as a foundation course giving direct, hands-on experience with GIS software for spatial-data analysis and display, and the department states its skills will be used to support upper-division courses, the clearest foundational-scaffolding statement in the whole program. The applied tasks, loading, symbolizing, querying, and analyzing spatial data in a GIS platform, are Computer and Mathematical work, the largest observed-usage category in current AI adoption data, and closely resemble the coding and data-manipulation tasks task-exposure research classifies as strongly exposed. At 24 months AI can already execute many discrete GIS operations, partially eroding the instrumental case for teaching students to perform them manually. But because this is the load-bearing prerequisite substrate for the entire upper-division geospatial curriculum, students must master the platform before they can direct or verify AI-assisted analysis later. The rating is Medium, capped by foundational role even as F1 exposure is already elevated.

By 2031, AI agents will likely execute most routine GIS operations, data management, spatial queries, basic analysis workflows, competently and with limited supervision, consistent with the capability trend of rapidly lengthening AI task-time-horizons. The perform-the-operations-yourself rationale weakens substantially. Yet GIS 2250 remains the explicit foundation course for the major: without hands-on platform fluency, students cannot specify, direct, or catch errors in AI-driven spatial analysis in later required courses like Cartography, Web Mapping, or Remote Sensing. The jagged-frontier evidence is directly relevant here, since users operating outside their competence with AI tools make more errors while trusting the output more, exactly the risk this foundation course is meant to prevent. The instrumental case shifts from perform-the-analysis to understand-the-platform-well-enough-to-verify-AI-output, and the foundational-scaffolding cap holds the rating at Medium rather than allowing it to rise to High.

A decade out, the central case has AI performing most standard GIS workflows, data preparation, spatial queries, basic modeling, with the human role shifting toward specification and verification of increasingly autonomous geospatial analysis. The execution-focused rationale for this course is substantially eroded. But GIS 2250's role as the load-bearing prerequisite for the entire upper-division geospatial-science sequence is a structural, not a capability-contingent, fact: as long as later courses assume GIS platform fluency, this course remains instrumentally necessary regardless of how far AI advances. The rating holds Medium, capped by foundational role rather than by any near-term limit on AI's GIS competence. The uncertainty concerns how the department restructures the introductory sequence once most execution is automated, not whether some foundational GIS literacy remains a prerequisite for students continuing into the applied and programming-heavy upper-division courses that depend on it.
GIS 2250.d: This is a foundation course that provides students with the basic knowledge of Geographic Information Systems (GIS) with regard to theoretical, technical, and application issues. It introduces and provides direct experience with the techniques used to analyze and display spatial data using GIS. The skills and knowledge developed in this course will be used to support upper-division courses.

r: GIS 2710 teaches land navigation using maps and handheld GPS units, with students physically navigating positions in the field and completing GPS lab and field exercises before integrating results with GIS. The core applied task, real-time, in-person navigation across physical terrain, is embodied and psychomotor, not the kind of digital knowledge work captured in observed-usage or task-exposure data, which finds manual and physical work consistently low-exposure. Whatever data-integration work follows, importing GPS tracks into GIS, is a minor, digital-only slice of the course. At 24 months, AI cannot stand in for a student walking a course with a GPS receiver, reading terrain, and correcting position in real time. The instrumental need to physically practice navigation is essentially untouched by current AI capability. The rating is Low, driven by embodiment rather than by any complexity in the underlying wayfinding concepts.

By 2031, consumer and field-navigation tools will likely be more capable and more integrated with GIS platforms, and the data-integration component of the course may see modest AI assistance. But the field-exercise core, physically navigating terrain with map and GPS receiver, reading the landscape, and correcting course in real time, remains an embodied, psychomotor skill outside what digital AI systems perform, consistent with the low exposure of manual and physical work in task-exposure research. Diffusion data shows AI adoption is uneven and lags capability even in office settings, and there is no comparable trend toward automating supervised in-person land-navigation instruction. The instrumental case for teaching this skill through direct field practice is not meaningfully eroded by AI capability gains over this horizon. The rating remains Low, hedged only by the possibility that GPS-to-GIS data-integration workflows shift somewhat toward automated tooling.

A decade out, the physical act of field navigation, walking positions, reading terrain, operating a receiver under real conditions, is not a task category where digital AI substitutes for embodied practice, regardless of how far model capability advances on the documented task-time-horizon trend. Robotic or autonomous navigation exists in other domains, but this course's instrumental purpose is the student's own embodied competence, not a navigation deliverable that could be handed to a model. The rating holds Low. The genuine long-horizon uncertainty concerns the digital data-integration and analysis component of the course, which could see further automation as GPS-to-GIS workflows mature, but that is a peripheral part of the course relative to the field-exercise core. This is a directional judgment given the ten-year distance, not a confident prediction, but embodiment is a structural rather than capability-contingent constraint here.
GIS 2710.d: This course is an introduction to the science of land navigation using maps and a Global Positioning System (GPS), Students navigate positions in the field and apply cartographic principles to GPS lab and field exercises. Emphasis is given to the integration of GPS data with Geographic Information Systems (GIS).

r: Cartography teaches students to critique and design cartographic products, choropleth, dot-density, contour, and proportional-symbol maps, and extends into web maps and animated temporal visualizations using GIS software. Map design and data visualization are squarely Computer and Mathematical work, the largest category in observed AI usage, and generative tools already produce competent draft visualizations and web-map code. At 24 months AI can generate serviceable map layouts and basic web-mapping scaffolding, partially eroding the instrumental need for students to produce these products manually. The course is a required contributor to the geospatial-science major without a hard accreditation floor, and its design skills feed a later directed-study option, giving it a modest but not decisive foundational role. The rating is Medium: exposure is real and rising, but near-term diffusion and the residual foundational contribution keep it from High at this horizon.

By 2031, AI will likely generate polished, publication-ready thematic maps, web-mapping applications, and animated visualizations from a data set and a brief description, substantially eroding the case for students to hand-design these products themselves. Task-exposure research classifies design and visualization work, closely related to writing and programming, among the more exposed activities, and the modest foundational contribution to later coursework only caps the rating at the 24-month horizon under the scoring rule, not beyond it. With no embodiment, licensure, or strong verification barrier specific to cartographic design, and only a partial major-contribution lock rather than a hard mandate, little protects the rating from rising. The instrumental case shifts toward critiquing, directing, and refining AI-generated cartographic output rather than producing it from scratch. The rating is High, reflecting substantially automatable applied work with the design-judgment residue no longer sufficient to hold it at Medium.

A decade out, the central case has AI producing sophisticated, interactive, and well-designed cartographic products essentially on demand, given the same capability trajectory that already makes visualization and code-generation tasks strongly exposed. The instrumental case for teaching manual map-design execution is substantially eroded; what would remain valuable is a smaller set of design-judgment and critique skills for evaluating whether an AI-generated map misleads or omits context, a narrower slice of the course's full content. No hard institutional or embodiment constraint protects this course at the ten-year horizon. The rating is High, hedged by genuine ten-year uncertainty about capability diffusion and by the possibility that cartographic critique retains a curatorial premium even as production automates. This is a directional call given the distance of the horizon, not a confident point-prediction about exactly how map-making instruction is restructured.
GIS 3250.d: This course focuses on basic cartographic and visualization concepts and techniques to convey spatial information. Students will critique and design basic cartographic products such as dot, choropleth, contour, and proportional symbol maps using Geographic Information Systems (GIS). They will explore advanced visualization techniques such as integrating data, text, and graphics, developing web maps, and animating maps to show temporal change. Cartographic applications for natural resource management and planning are stressed.

r: Web Mapping has students design, develop, and implement web-mapping applications with ESRI and open-source tools, write basic JavaScript, and work with distributed and cloud-computing concepts; this is applied software development, not just GIS operation. Coding is the most exposed task category in the evidence base: it anchors the largest share of observed AI usage, and controlled studies show large developer-productivity gains from AI coding assistance. At 24 months AI already scaffolds JavaScript web-mapping code competently, partially eroding the instrumental case for students to write it unaided. The course lacks embodiment, has no accreditation-specific mandate, and only partially contributes to major requirements. The rating is Medium at this horizon primarily because near-term diffusion is uneven, Census data shows a modest share of firms actively using AI in production, even though the underlying task type is already highly automatable in principle.

By 2031, AI coding assistants will very likely handle most of the JavaScript, API integration, and cloud-deployment work this course teaches, consistent with GitHub Copilot-scale productivity gains already observed and the rapid task-time-horizon growth documented in capability-trend research. The rationale for hand-writing web-mapping application code weakens sharply. Nothing in the course carries embodiment, licensure, or a hard accreditation floor, and it is not a hard prerequisite for other required courses, so little caps the rating as exposure rises. The instrumental case shifts from writing web-mapping code to specifying application requirements and verifying that AI-generated spatial-data-infrastructure implementations behave correctly, a real but substantially narrower competence than full-course content. The rating is High: the applied development work is largely automatable, with the residual concentrated in direction and verification rather than hands-on coding.

A decade out, AI systems building complete web-mapping applications from a specification is a plausible central case, given how strongly programming tasks are positioned on the exposure spectrum and the trajectory of AI coding capability. The course's execution-oriented content, writing JavaScript, wiring APIs, configuring cloud deployment, is substantially eroded as an instrumental necessity. The residual is specification and verification skill: knowing enough about spatial data infrastructure and web architecture to direct and check an AI-built application, a smaller slice of the full course. No institutional or embodiment constraint holds the rating down at this horizon. The rating is High, hedged by the customary ten-year uncertainty about diffusion speed and by the possibility that spatial-web-architecture literacy retains value as an oversight skill even after routine implementation automates.
GIS 3410.d: This course is an introduction to creating web mapping applications on the Internet and serves as an introduction to Spatial Data Infrastructures. Students design, develop, and implement web mapping applications using ESRI software and open source software. Students work with web authoring tools, learn basic javascript, and work with basic visualization tools. Lectures focus on the theories and principles behind web mapping, distributed and cloud computing, graphic design, and other principles of web-based cartography.

r: GIS 3920 is an independent-study vehicle: students propose milestones and deliverables with a faculty advisor to pursue original research, a self-directed project, or assistance on a faculty research project in geospatial sciences. Because the actual work is defined per student, the applied tasks vary, literature synthesis, GIS analysis, data processing, or fieldwork assistance, but the description itself weights toward research design, data analysis, and documentation, which are Computer and Mathematical and writing-adjacent tasks in the exposed range of observed AI usage. At 24 months AI competently assists with research framing, data-analysis scripting, and drafting deliverables, partially eroding the instrumental case for doing this work unaided, though real diffusion into supervised independent-study courses lags. The rating is Medium, held with lower confidence than course-specific ratings because the generic, student-defined content makes any single task mapping only approximate.

By 2031, AI will likely handle much of the analytical and drafting work that independent-study projects in geospatial sciences typically involve, literature review, data processing, exploratory analysis, and report writing, consistent with the broader productivity gains documented for professional writing and analytical tasks. Because this course has no accreditation floor, no embodiment requirement, and only a weak prerequisite dependency on Cartography, little structurally caps the rating as the underlying task types become more automatable. The instrumental case shifts toward problem framing, oversight of AI-assisted research, and faculty-directed judgment calls that a template course description cannot fully specify. The rating is High, held with continued lower confidence: the actual balance of embodied fieldwork versus digital analysis in any given directed-study project is unknown from the catalog description alone, and that variability is a genuine source of uncertainty distinct from the AI-capability hedge.

A decade out, if directed-study projects in geospatial sciences continue to emphasize data analysis, modeling, and written research deliverables, the parts of the generic description most amenable to inference, AI is a plausible central-case collaborator or primary executor for much of that work, given the capability trajectory documented across programming, writing, and analytical tasks. The rating is High, but confidence remains low: this course's content is defined anew by each student and advisor, so the ten-year projection compounds normal capability uncertainty with description-level uncertainty about what any given enrollment actually entails. Some directed studies could involve substantial embodied fieldwork that would behave more like the program's field-based courses; the catalog text does not resolve this. The rating should be read as a best estimate for the modal case described, not a confident claim about every possible instantiation of this course.
GIS 3920.d: This course provides an opportunity for upper-division students to independently study a specific topic, initiate their own research or creative project, or assist with a research project initiated by a faculty member in the Geospatial Sciences. Proposals including expected milestones and deliverables will be developed in cooperation with a faculty advisor. The course requires permission of the instructor to enroll.

r: Environmental Hazards and GIS evaluates hazards relative to land-use patterns, using case studies and GIS to examine hazards and build predictive models, spatial modeling and analysis work that is Computer and Mathematical in character and squarely in the exposed range of observed AI usage. But this course's deliverables, hazard models, land-use risk assessments, are the kind of output that informs real regulatory, planning, and safety decisions, which raises the verification burden: the jagged-frontier evidence shows AI users outside their competence trust flawed output at elevated rates, and hazard misclassification carries real consequences rather than being merely inconvenient. At 24 months AI can assist with GIS-based hazard modeling, but the instrumental need for a human who understands the modeling assumptions well enough to catch a flawed hazard assessment before it informs a planning decision is not eroded. The rating is Low, driven by verification burden rather than exposure.

By 2031, AI will likely generate sophisticated hazard models and land-use risk analyses rapidly, and the routine GIS-modeling workload of this course becomes substantially automatable, consistent with the broader trend of AI performing applied spatial-analysis tasks competently. The rating rises to Medium. But the verification burden persists as a structural constraint rather than disappearing with capability: hazard assessments feed consequential regulatory and public-safety decisions, and the jagged-frontier finding that miscalibrated trust in AI output is common outside a user's expertise applies directly to a domain where a flawed flood or seismic-risk model has real downstream costs. The instrumental case shifts from producing hazard models to critically evaluating model assumptions and outputs before they inform decisions, a genuine competency this course teaches, which caps the rating below where pure task-exposure would otherwise place it.

A decade out, AI hazard-modeling and land-use risk-assessment tools are plausibly very capable, and the execution-focused rationale for teaching students to build these models by hand is substantially eroded. Yet the verification-burden constraint is durable rather than capability-contingent: as long as hazard assessments carry real consequences for public safety and land-use policy, someone with domain expertise needs to catch non-obvious model failures before they propagate into decisions, and that is precisely the oversight competency this course cultivates. The rating holds Medium, capped by verification burden rather than by any near-term limit on AI capability. This is a hedged, directional judgment at ten years; the pace of institutional adoption of AI hazard tools in regulatory contexts specifically is uncertain, and diffusion research shows adoption of AI generally lags well behind raw capability even in less consequential domains.
GIS 4010.d: This course evaluates environmental hazards relative to various land-use patterns. It utilizes case studies and Geographical Information Systems (GIS) to examine hazards and prepare models.

r: Landscape Ecology examines how spatial pattern and scale shape ecological processes, and connects those concepts to environmental policy, management, regulation, and assessment, while building geospatial-analysis skills with GIS tools. The course blends scientific and ecological reasoning, a category task-exposure research finds strongly negatively associated with AI exposure, with applied geospatial data analysis, which sits in the more exposed Computer and Mathematical category. That mix keeps the rating from moving as quickly as a purely technical GIS course. At 24 months, AI can process spatial data and compute standard landscape metrics, but the ecological interpretation connecting pattern, scale, and policy implications draws on scientific judgment that current models handle less reliably. The rating is Medium: the geospatial-tooling component is meaningfully exposed, while the ecological-reasoning core provides real, if partial, protection against a higher rating.

By 2031, AI will likely handle most of the mechanical geospatial-analysis workload, computing landscape metrics, processing spatial pattern data, competently, but the course's core intellectual content, connecting ecological process to spatial pattern and translating that into policy and management recommendations, remains scientific and critical-thinking work that task-exposure research consistently finds less exposed than routine technical tasks. The rating holds Medium rather than rising to High: the applied tooling erodes toward automation, but the ecological-scientific reasoning that gives the geospatial output meaning is not simply a data-processing task and resists full delegation to AI at this horizon. This is a genuine, if narrowing, distinction from purely technical GIS courses like Cartography or Web Mapping, whose content maps more directly onto exposed programming and design tasks.

A decade out, the distinction between technical geospatial tooling and ecological-scientific reasoning may narrow further as AI models improve at scientific inference generally, and the central case has AI handling a much larger share of both the spatial-analysis workload and the interpretive synthesis connecting landscape pattern to policy outcomes. The rating rises to High, reflecting substantial erosion of the instrumental case across the course's full scope. This is hedged more than the near-term ratings: the negative association between scientific and critical-thinking skills and AI exposure found in current task-exposure research may not hold as strongly a decade out if model scientific reasoning keeps improving at the pace suggested by capability-trend research, but that improvement is not guaranteed, and the ecological-judgment component could retain more residual value than the rating implies.
GIS 4400.d: Students will examine the effects of spatial pattern and scale on ecological processes and learn how the concepts of landscape ecology apply to environmental policy, management, regulation, and assessment. Students will develop skills for geospatial analysis of data using various geospatial tools.

r: GIS Programming teaches Python scripting and object-oriented programming within the ArcGIS environment, with students writing structured programs to manage geospatial data, automate geoprocessing, and script mapping and visualization tasks; this is coding, full stop, applied to a spatial-data domain. Programming is the single most exposed task type in the evidence base: it anchors the largest observed-usage category, and controlled studies on GitHub Copilot document large speed gains from AI coding assistance. At 24 months AI already writes competent Python geoprocessing scripts from a description of the task, substantially eroding the instrumental case for a student to write basic automation scripts unaided. The rating is Medium at this horizon primarily because of near-term diffusion lag into course-level instruction and assessment redesign, not because the underlying scripting tasks resist automation; they do not.

By 2031, AI coding assistants will very likely write, debug, and explain ArcGIS Python automation scripts as well as or better than an entry-level student, consistent with the strong and persistent positive association between programming tasks and AI exposure found in task-exposure research. Nothing in this course carries embodiment, licensure, or an accreditation-specific credit-hour floor, and it is not a hard prerequisite for other required courses, so no structural cap holds the rating down as capability rises. The instrumental case shifts from writing geoprocessing scripts to specifying automation requirements and verifying that AI-generated scripts correctly manipulate spatial data, a real but substantially narrower skill than the full course. The rating is High: the applied programming work this course teaches is largely performed competently by AI with limited need for a human to write it from scratch.

A decade out, AI systems generating and debugging GIS automation scripts from natural-language specifications is a plausible central case, extending the same trajectory that already makes coding the most exposed task category in the evidence base. The course's execution-oriented content, writing and structuring Python programs, is substantially eroded as an instrumental necessity; what would remain is the ability to specify geoprocessing requirements precisely and verify AI-generated automation before it runs against production spatial data. No institutional or embodiment constraint protects this course at the ten-year horizon. The rating is High, hedged by standard ten-year uncertainty about the pace of capability diffusion into specialized domains like ArcGIS scripting specifically, and by the possibility that scripting literacy retains value as a verification skill even after most routine automation is AI-generated.
GIS 4810.n: September 2026 evidence update. Task automatability (F1) raised at 24 months from 3 to 4. Python scripting in ArcGIS to manage geospatial data and automate geoprocessing and mapping tasks, which is routine scripting. Stanford's August 2026 payroll update places software developers and computer programmers in the most AI-exposed occupations, where employment of 22-to-25-year-olds is 19% below trend, mainly through reduced hiring; the Bureau of Labor Statistics' 2025-35 projections put computer programmers at -7.3%. Both are descriptive signals, not proof that AI caused the decline. Rating changed (24 months: Medium to High); confidence lowered one step because the supporting labor data are descriptive. The original paragraph below is retained for transparency.
GIS 4810.d: This course is an introduction to programming and scripting for intermediate Geographic Information Systems (GIS) users. The fundamental concepts of scripting and object-oriented programming will be developed using the Python programming language. This course teaches students to design and write clearly structured programs in Python in the ArcGIS environment. Students will develop programs to manage geospatial data, perform geoprocessing analysis to solve spatial problems, and automate mapping and visualization tasks.

r: Remote Sensing covers photogrammetry, the interaction of electromagnetic radiation with Earth's surface, and interpretation of aerial and satellite imagery across multispectral, thermal-infrared, and microwave bands, with students performing digital image-processing operations in specialized software. Image classification and interpretation from satellite and aerial imagery is a well-established strength of machine-learning systems, and this technical, data-processing work falls squarely in the Computer and Mathematical category that dominates observed AI usage. At 24 months AI-assisted classification and feature extraction from remote-sensing imagery already performs many of these interpretation tasks competently, partially eroding the instrumental case for manual digital image processing. The physics-principles component, radiation-surface interaction, requires some conceptual grounding, but the applied processing workflow is highly automatable. The rating is Medium, reflecting real near-term exposure tempered by uneven diffusion of specialized remote-sensing AI tools into instructional settings.

By 2031, AI-based image classification and multispectral or thermal image processing will likely handle most of the applied interpretation work this course teaches, extending the well-documented strength of machine-learning systems at exactly this kind of pattern-recognition task. No embodiment, licensure, or accreditation-specific credit floor protects the course, and it is not a hard prerequisite for other required coursework, so little caps the rating as the underlying image-processing tasks become more automatable. The instrumental case shifts from manually classifying and processing imagery to specifying analysis parameters and verifying that AI-driven classification and change-detection outputs are physically and geographically sound, a real but narrower competency than the full course. The rating is High: the applied remote-sensing workflow is largely automatable, with the physics-grounded verification role as the more durable residual.

A decade out, AI systems performing end-to-end remote-sensing analysis, from raw imagery to classified, change-detected outputs, is a plausible central case, given how strongly image-processing and pattern-recognition tasks already sit within AI's demonstrated strengths and the broader capability trajectory documented in task-time-horizon research. The course's execution-oriented content, digital image-processing operations, is substantially eroded as an instrumental necessity. What would remain is the physics and sensor-principles literacy needed to specify appropriate imagery, interpret edge cases, and catch non-obvious classification errors, a smaller residual than the full course content. No institutional or embodiment constraint holds the rating down at this horizon. The rating is High, hedged by the customary ten-year uncertainty and by the possibility that sensor-physics grounding retains value as a verification skill in specialized applications like defense, agriculture, or disaster response.
GIS 4840.d: Students are introduced to the principles and techniques of photogrammetry and remote sensing, along with their applications in environmental and land management contexts. Students examine the interaction of electromagnetic radiation with Earth's surface materials and the atmosphere, and learn how these principles inform the interpretation of aerial and satellite imagery. Topics include electromagnetic radiation principles, aerial photography, multi- spectral remote sensing, thermal infrared remote sensing, active and passive microwave remote sensing, and remote sensing applications. Students learn fundamental remote sensing and digital image processing operations using state-of-the-art remote sensing software packages.

r: This upper-division course applies map algebra and raster procedures to land-use planning and natural-resource decision support, tasks that map onto analyzing data, interacting with computers, and evaluating information against planning standards. Current geospatial AI assistants can already draft raster overlay scripts and automate routine map-algebra steps, and observed-usage data shows Computer & Mathematical activity dominating consumer and API traffic, suggesting adjacent tooling is diffusing into GIS workflows. Still, translating a raster model into a defensible land-use or resource-management recommendation requires judgment about local context, data provenance, and stakeholder tradeoffs that off-the-shelf tools do not reliably supply. Diffusion data indicate only a minority of firms have operationalized AI tools this specifically by now, and instructor-guided practice in this course still trains skills current systems apply unevenly. The instrumental need to take this course remains real but is narrowing as scripting assistance matures around its procedural core.

By the five-year horizon, map-algebra scripting and standard raster workflows (overlay, reclassification, cost-distance modeling) are plausibly routine for AI-assisted geoprocessing, since task-exposure research classifies programming-adjacent, well-specified procedures as strongly positively exposed. Land-use planning and natural-resource applications built on raster outputs would likely rely on AI to generate first-pass models, with a human analyst validating assumptions and calibrating parameters to local site conditions. Capability-trend evidence describing rapid doubling of task-time horizons supports continued gains in handling multi-step spatial modeling reliably. Verification burden stays real, however, because planning decisions carry real consequences and errors in raster logic are not always obvious without domain expertise, so the jagged-frontier finding about miscalibrated trust cautions against assuming full automation. This pushes the course toward a High rating while leaving open how much hands-on modeling training remains instrumentally necessary for competent oversight.

Ten years out, raster modeling and map-algebra procedures for land-use and natural-resource applications are likely well within AI competence, especially as compute continues scaling and specialized geospatial-AI tooling matures alongside general-purpose assistants. Whether this fully displaces the instrumental need for structured coursework is harder to state with confidence, since diffusion research shows adoption of AI tools lags well behind raw capability, and much land-use and resource-management practice occurs inside slower-moving public agencies and planning bodies. Applied decision-support work also draws on locally specific ecological and regulatory knowledge that generic models handle unevenly, keeping some verification burden intact even as routine modeling steps become largely automatable. Given the pattern of upper-division applied GIS courses documented across this discipline, a High rating is defensible, but any ten-year projection here carries meaningful uncertainty about institutional and workplace adoption pace.
GIS 4850.d: This is an upper-division course in Geographic Information Systems (GIS) with an emphasis on spatial analysis and modeling. The underlying foundations of map algebra are discussed along with practical exercises that allow the student to develop familiarity with those procedures. This course offers an opportunity for students with a solid background in the fundamentals of GIS to apply the analytical capabilities of this technology to model real- world situations in support of decision-making. Application of GIS to the fields of Land Use Planning and Natural Resource Management are emphasized.

r: This course trains vector-data modeling, spatial analysis, and project management using ArcGIS and Arc/Info, culminating in a student-designed application project, work mapping to interacting with computers, analyzing data, and organizing and prioritizing work. Much of the software mechanics (attribute editing, geodatabase structuring, basic spatial queries) already overlaps with tasks AI coding and data assistants handle competently, consistent with task-exposure research linking programming-adjacent activities to strong positive exposure. But conceiving and managing an original GIS application, choosing an appropriate data model, and defending design tradeoffs remain squarely instructor-guided skills at this stage, and observed-usage patterns show augmentation rather than full task replacement dominating current consumer use. As a prerequisite gateway feeding several later upper-division GIS courses, the course also carries scaffolding weight that keeps its near-term instrumental value from collapsing even as individual software tasks become more automatable.

Within five years, AI copilots embedded in GIS platforms are likely to routinely handle vector-data model selection scaffolding, geodatabase setup, and much of the mechanical analysis this course teaches, aligning with productivity-RCT findings that coding-adjacent assistance produces large task-speed gains for practitioners. The original-project requirement, however, still demands synthesizing project management, data design, and applied judgment that generalist tools apply unevenly outside well-specified problems, per the jagged-frontier research on inconsistent AI performance beyond its competence frontier. Because this course remains a prerequisite for Spatial Databases, the capstone project course, and satellite image analysis within this program, its foundational role partially insulates it from a full automatability rating even as its component tasks individually trend toward High exposure. A High rating is reasonable for the technical content, tempered by continued scaffolding value for the major's later coursework.

At ten years, vector GIS software operations and standard spatial-analysis workflows plausibly sit deep inside AI competence, given the compute and capability trends documented in task-time-horizon research, though translating that into full displacement of this course is speculative. The course's role as a prerequisite for three further upper-division GIS courses in this curriculum means its instrumental value is partly structural rather than purely task-based, and macro-level productivity evidence suggests aggregate effects of AI diffusion remain modest even over a decade. Original project design, stakeholder-facing project management, and defending data-model choices likely retain a verification and judgment component that generic automation handles unevenly. A High rating captures the technical trajectory, but the scaffolding role this course plays for later coursework argues for caution in treating that rating as a confident forecast of the course disappearing from the curriculum.
GIS 4860.d: This course provides advanced theoretical and practical knowledge in Geographic Information Systems (GIS), with emphasis on vector data models.
